title: If diplomacy has value, Prabowo needs to show the numbers
gist: Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto's overseas trips have generated roughly US$136 billion (Rp 2,430 trillion) in claimed investment over 18 months, but these are pledges and MoUs, not realised capital — Japan pledged US$23 billion after the March Tokyo trip against just US$3.1 billion of realised Japanese investment in all of 2025. The author argues Indonesia already has the institutional machinery (BKPM, Danantara, Foreign Ministry, Finance) to publish a post-trip scorecard on disbursement, implementation and cost, and that the absence of one is a habit problem rather than a data problem.

insights.claim: Indonesia's headline investment figures from presidential travel — US$23 billion from Tokyo, US$10 billion from Seoul, US$18 billion combined from London and Beijing — are pledges and memoranda of understanding announced at forums and rarely revisited, not committed capital.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Discount Indonesian state-visit investment headlines heavily when modelling FDI inflows; MoU totals are a marketing number, not a pipeline.
insights.quote: They are pledges and memoranda of understanding, announced at forums and rarely revisited.
insights.locator: The trouble is that almost none of these numbers

insights.claim: The US$23 billion Japan pledged after Prabowo's March 2026 Tokyo trip compares with realised Japanese investment in Indonesia of just US$3.1 billion for the whole of 2025 — roughly a sevenfold gap between announcement and delivery.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: A concrete conversion benchmark: use realised-to-pledged ratios of this order when hazarding what Indonesian summit announcements actually deliver.

insights.claim: Prabowo's cabinet secretary cited Investment Coordinating Board data in June claiming presidential travel had brought in roughly Rp 2,430 trillion — about US$136 billion — in 18 months.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: This is the official number that will anchor Indonesian growth and FDI narratives; know that it aggregates unrealised pledges before citing it.

insights.claim: The pattern predates Prabowo: under Joko Widodo, headline investment figures from state visits routinely dwarfed what eventually showed up as realised investment.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: This is a structural feature of Indonesian economic diplomacy across administrations, not an artefact of one president — apply the discount persistently.
insights.quote: Under President Joko Widodo, headline investment figures from state visits routinely dwarfed what eventually showed up as realised investment.

insights.claim: Part of the gap is legitimate — big energy projects take years to build — but the delay itself makes the announcement-to-delivery gap difficult for the public to track.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Long project lead times give governments indefinite cover for unrealised pledges; time-stamped realisation data is the only way to separate slow from stalled.
insights.quote: Big energy projects take years to build.
insights.locator: Big energy projects take years to build

insights.claim: Since taking office in October 2024, Prabowo has visited at least 29 countries across more than 50 overseas engagements and, by one count, spent at least 99 days abroad on official visits.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Roughly a fifth of the presidency spent overseas is a measurable claim on executive bandwidth — relevant to the pace of domestic reform delivery in Indonesia.
insights.quote: Prabowo has visited at least 29 countries (Opens in new window) in more than 50 overseas engagements, and by one count has spent at least 99 days abroad on official visits
insights.locator: The scale of the travel behind these numbers

insights.claim: Criticism of the travel pace is coming from inside Indonesia's foreign policy establishment, with Foreign Policy Community of Indonesia founder Dino Patti Djalal arguing in May that the pace had become difficult to justify.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Elite-level scepticism of Prabowo's economic diplomacy is now public, a marker of domestic political friction around the administration's flagship narrative.
insights.locator: In May this year, the Foreign Policy Community

insights.claim: The administration's fiscal defence — aide Teddy Indra Wijaya's claim that excess state-budget costs are borne personally by Prabowo — is as unverifiable as the investment figures, with no published breakdown of trip costs or personal coverage.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Both sides of Indonesia's presidential-travel debate rest on unauditable assertions — a governance-transparency signal that extends beyond travel to how state figures are presented generally.
insights.quote: any excess costs from the state budget are entirely borne by President Prabowo himself.
insights.locator: Aide Teddy Indra Wijaya defended it

insights.claim: The entire debate over Prabowo's travel is being conducted with unverifiable headline claims on both sides, leaving the public asked to take assertions on faith about both investment and spending.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Absence of verifiable data — not disagreement over the data — is the binding constraint; expect the dispute to persist unresolved without a disclosure change.
insights.quote: The debate over Prabowo’s travel is being fought entirely with unverifiable headline claims on both sides.

insights.claim: The author proposes a standing post-trip scorecard covering disbursed investment, agreements moved into implementation, agreements that lapsed, jobs created, technology transfer, trip cost and any personal coverage — with a public timeline and named responsible ministries.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: A reusable template for evaluating any government's economic-diplomacy claims: demand disbursed-versus-pledged, implementation status, and lapse rate.
insights.quote: how much announced investment has been disbursed, which agreements have moved into implementation, and which have lapsed

insights.claim: Indonesia already has the institutional machinery to produce such a report — BKPM tracks realised versus pledged investment, Danantara was launched precisely to convert pledges into projects, the Foreign Ministry keeps agreement records, and Finance accounts for travel budgets.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Danantara's mandate is explicitly pledge-to-project conversion, making its disclosed pipeline the single best proxy for whether Indonesia's headline FDI numbers are real.
insights.quote: What is missing is not data, but a habit of publishing it

insights.claim: A government confident in its own numbers has every incentive to publish follow-through data, so continued reliance on unverifiable totals is itself evidence about the underlying figures.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Treat non-disclosure as informative: the longer Jakarta withholds realisation data, the more the pledge headlines should be discounted.
insights.quote: If the numbers hold up, the government has nothing to fear from publishing them.
insights.locator: This is not an argument about whether Prabowo travels too often

insights.claim: Indonesia's push for foreign investors to process raw materials domestically only works if capital actually arrives and plants get built, making realisation data a direct test of the downstreaming policy rather than a mere accountability nicety.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Indonesia's commodity-processing thesis — nickel and other downstreaming plays — depends on pledge conversion; ceremonial totals are not evidence the plants exist.
insights.quote: Indonesia’s push for foreign investors to process raw materials domestically will only work if capital actually arrives and plants get built.
insights.locator: There is a diplomatic case too

insights.claim: Publishing realisation data against commitments would reveal which foreign partners actually follow through, giving Jakarta better negotiating leverage than a tally of ceremonial totals.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Country-level conversion rates would be a genuinely tradeable dataset — identifying which of Japan, Korea, the UK or China actually deploys capital into Indonesia.
insights.quote: Realisation data published against commitments would show which partners are following through – better leverage than a tally of ceremonial totals.

insights.claim: Foreign trips consume presidential time, cabinet attention and travel budgets that could go elsewhere, so the opportunity cost stands regardless of what the optimal travel frequency turns out to be.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Frames the trade-off in resource terms rather than political ones — useful when assessing whether an administration's external focus is crowding out domestic execution.
insights.quote: Foreign trips consume presidential time, cabinet attention and travel budgets that could go elsewhere, whatever the right frequency of travel turns out to be.
